## Creating reproducible reports in R ##

Welcome to the final week of the bootcamp! In Week 1 we typed commands into the console. Last week we saved those commands into a script so that anyone could rerun them and get exactly the same plots and tables every time. That was a big step forward, but think about what happens when you need to write up your results. You run your script, open Word, paste your plots in and then copy the numbers from the console into your sentences by hand. Now imagine you find a mistake in your script, or your supervisor asks you to try a different parameter value. Every plot and every number in that Word document is now wrong and you have to hunt down and fix each one by hand. Miss one and your report contradicts itself. Not a good look.

So how do we get around this I hear you ask? Great question! This week we are tackling ``R Markdown``. An R Markdown document is a single file that holds your writing, your code and the results of that code (numbers, tables and plots) all together. When you click ``Knit``, R runs every bit of code in the document from top to bottom and builds a finished report, which in our case will be a Word document. Change a number in your code, knit again, and every plot, table and sentence that depends on it updates itself. This idea of weaving code and writing together into the one document is called **literate programming**.

Here's a fun fact for you. Every tutorial page you've read in this bootcamp, including this one, is an R Markdown document. If you'd like to see what this page looks like before it's knitted, you can download its source file, [week_3.Rmd](week_3.Rmd), and open it in RStudio.

**This week, the report you produce is your assessment item.** First we'll learn how R Markdown works. Then, just like you built a script last week, you'll build a report as you work through the tutorial. It tells the story of a coral trout fishery that was fished almost to collapse, closed for 40 years to let it recover, and now wants to reopen. Using 40 years of survey data, you'll work out how the population grows and recommend how many fish can be harvested each year without it collapsing again. The checklist for your report is in the [assessment section](#your-assessment) at the bottom of this page.

## Setting up ##

As always, we start by creating a new project for this tutorial. Choose a logical location and name, just like you did in the last two weeks.

```{r eval=FALSE}
# !!Remember to change these paths to suit your own directory structure!!

# On Mac or Linux
dir.create("~/Documents/teaching/2026/TR3/SC1102/SC1102_tut3", recursive = TRUE)

# On Windows (keep your work in C:/RWork, outside OneDrive)
dir.create("C:/RWork/SC1102/SC1102_tut3", recursive = TRUE)

```

Then click ``File``/``New Project...``/``Existing Directory``, browse to your new ``SC1102_tut3`` folder and click ``Create Project``.

R Markdown needs a package called ``rmarkdown``. RStudio usually offers to install it for you the first time you make an R Markdown file, but if it doesn't, run this once in the console.

```{r eval=FALSE}
# Install the rmarkdown package. You only need to do this once on each computer
install.packages("rmarkdown")

```

### Your first R Markdown document ###

1. Click ``File``/``New File``/``R Markdown...``
2. In the window that pops up, choose ``Document`` on the left. Give it the title ``Reopening the coral trout fishery``, put your name in as the author, and under ``Default Output Format`` choose ``Word``. Click ``OK``.
3. A new file opens in the top left pane. It isn't empty, RStudio has filled it with an example to get you started.
4. Save it straight away into your project folder with ``File``/``Save As``. Use the same naming scheme as last week, so mine is ``adc_sc1102_tut3.Rmd``. Note the file extension is ``.Rmd`` and not ``.R``.

**SUPER ULTRA CRITICAL REMINDER HERE!!** This week everything you do goes into your R Markdown document, not the console. If you just run commands in the console, they won't end up in your report, and if they're not in your report, you'll have nothing to submit!

Now, before you change anything, click the ``Knit`` button (the ball of wool with a needle through it) at the top of the file. RStudio will run the document and a Word document will pop up, complete with headings, text, code, a summary table and a plot. You'll also find the new ``.docx`` file sitting in your project folder right next to your ``.Rmd``. If you don't have Microsoft Word, you can open the ``.docx`` with LibreOffice, Pages or Google Docs.

And that's it, you've just made your first report! Now let's work out what's actually in the file.

## Anatomy of an R Markdown document ##

Every R Markdown document has three ingredients:

```
1. A YAML header   the settings for the document, between two lines of ---
2. Text            your writing, formatted with a simple system called Markdown
3. Code chunks     blocks of R code that run when you knit
```

### The YAML header ###

The block at the very top of your file, fenced off by two lines of ``---``, is called the YAML header (YAML rhymes with camel). It holds the settings for the whole document. Yours will look something like this:

```
---
title: "Reopening the coral trout fishery"
author: "Your Name"
date: "2026-10-27"
output: word_document
---
```

``output: word_document`` is the line that tells R to build a Word document. If you change it to ``output: html_document`` and knit, you get a web page instead. Same file, different output. YAML is fussy about spacing, so keep a space after each colon and keep text in quotation marks.

### Text and Markdown ###

Anything outside the YAML header and the code chunks is just text, and it ends up in your report as written. You format it with a handful of symbols called Markdown:

| You type | You get |
|---|---|
| ``# Introduction`` | A level 1 heading |
| ``## Methods`` | A level 2 heading |
| ``**important**`` | **important** |
| ``*Paramecium aurelia*`` | *Paramecium aurelia* |
| ``- an item`` (on its own line) | a bullet point |
| ``1. an item`` (on its own line) | a numbered list |
| ``$N_{t+1} = N_t + G(N_t) - h$`` | an equation, $N_{t+1} = N_t + G(N_t) - h$ |

Two things trip people up. First, you need a **blank line** between paragraphs, and before and after a list or heading, otherwise Markdown glues them together. Second, a ``#`` means something different depending on where it is. In the text, it makes a heading. Inside a code chunk, it's an R comment, just like in your scripts.

You may notice ``Source`` and ``Visual`` buttons at the top left of your file. Stay in ``Source`` mode for this tutorial so that what you see matches these instructions.

### Code chunks ###

A code chunk is a block of R code fenced off by three backticks. It looks like this in your ``.Rmd`` file:

````md
`r ''````{r}
# Calculate the maximum sustainable yield
MSY <- 0.2 * 100 / 4
MSY
```
````

The ``{r}`` tells R Markdown that the code inside is R code. When you knit, the code and its output both appear in the report. To add a new chunk, click ``Code``/``Insert Chunk``, or use the keyboard shortcut ``Ctrl + Alt + I`` (Windows and Linux) or ``Cmd + Option + I`` (Mac). Don't try to type the backticks yourself. They're easy to get wrong and on some keyboards they're hard to find.

While you're writing, you don't need to knit every time you want to test something. Each chunk has a little green play button at its top right that runs just that chunk, and its output appears right underneath. This works just like running lines from your script last week.

### Chunk options ###

You can control what each chunk shows in the final report by adding **chunk options** inside the curly braces, after the ``r``. You can also give a chunk a name, which makes it much easier to find where an error happened when knitting fails.

````md
`r ''````{r production-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="The logistic production function."}
```
````

These are the options you'll use most:

| Option | What it does |
|---|---|
| ``echo=FALSE`` | runs the code and shows the result, but hides the code |
| ``eval=FALSE`` | shows the code, but doesn't run it |
| ``include=FALSE`` | runs the code, but shows nothing at all |
| ``message=FALSE`` | hides the messages some functions print |
| ``warning=FALSE`` | hides warnings (use with care, warnings are often important!) |
| ``fig.cap="..."`` | adds a caption under a figure |
| ``fig.width=6, fig.height=4`` | sets the size of a figure, in inches |

Have a look at the first chunk in your file, the one called ``setup``. It has ``include=FALSE`` so it runs but never shows up in your report. The line inside, ``knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)``, sets the default for every chunk in the document so that your code is shown. Leave it as it is. For your assessment, the marker needs to see your code.

### Inline code ###

This is the feature that makes R Markdown so powerful. As well as chunks, you can put a small piece of R code straight into a sentence by writing a backtick, the letter ``r``, a space, your code, and a closing backtick. When you knit, the code is replaced by its result. So if you write this in the text part of your document:

````md
The maximum sustainable yield is `r knitr::inline_expr("MSY")` fish per year.
````

your Word document will say "The maximum sustainable yield is 5 fish per year." Change the parameters and knit again, and the sentence updates itself. **From now on, you should never type a number into your writing that R has calculated for you.** Use inline code instead.

### Knitting starts from scratch ###

This is the single most important thing to understand about R Markdown, so read this bit twice. When you click ``Knit``, R does **not** use anything in your Environment pane. It starts a brand new, empty R session, runs every chunk in your document in order from top to bottom, and builds the report from that. It's exactly the ``Restart R`` and ``Source`` test from last week, done for you automatically every time you knit.

This has some consequences:

- If you created a variable by typing in the console, but never put that code in a chunk, knitting will fail with ``Error: object 'something' not found``. The fix is to put the code in a chunk.
- Chunks run in order. If a chunk uses a variable, the chunk that creates it has to come first.
- Any files your document reads must be in the same folder as your ``.Rmd``.
- If you load a package with ``library()``, it has to be in a chunk too.

My advice is to **knit early and knit often**. If you knit after every new chunk or two, then when something breaks you'll know exactly which bit of code caused it. If you write the whole thing and only knit at the end, you'll be hunting through all of it at 11pm the night before it's due. Future you will thank past you for knitting often.

### Clear out the example ###

This document is going to become your report, so delete everything in your file **below** the ``setup`` chunk. Keep the YAML header and the setup chunk. Then knit again to check it still works. From here on, every chunk of code in this tutorial goes into your report, in order, and you'll write the text around it. Knit after every chunk or two.

## The story ##

Here's the situation. A coral trout fishery off the Queensland coast was fished so hard through the 1970s and early 80s that by 1985 the stock had crashed to a fraction of its former size. If fishing had carried on, the stock would almost certainly have collapsed altogether. So in 1985 fishing was banned, and every year since then, scientists have surveyed the number of coral trout in four zones of the fishery. Forty years on, the stock looks a lot healthier and the fishing industry wants to know if it can reopen.

That's where you come in. Your job is to use the survey data to work out how this population grows, and then to recommend a harvest that the fishery can sustain. Sound familiar? It's the same modelling cycle we used last week:

```
1. Question                 How much can we harvest each year without the stock collapsing?
2. Variables & assumptions  Population size N, harvest h, logistic growth
3. Model construction       N(t+1) = N(t) + G(N(t)) - h
4. Results                  Estimate K and R0 from the survey data, then G(N) and the MSY
5. Testability              Simulate the stock under different harvests
6. Evaluation               Which harvests are sustainable?
7. Interpretation           What harvest do we recommend?
```

**A word of warning, these data are simulated.** I made them up using the logistic model you've been building in this course, plus some random good and bad years, and some survey error to make them look like real survey data. Coral trout are real but this fishery and these numbers are not, so please don't quote them anywhere!

Every chunk from here on goes into your report. Where you see **In your report:**, that's something you need to write yourself.

Remember the general framework from the lectures. Next year's population is this year's population, plus natural population growth, minus the harvest:

$$N_{t+1} = N_t + G(N_t) - h$$

and for logistic growth, the production function is:

$$G(N) = R_0\left(1 - \frac{N}{K}\right)N$$

**In your report:** under a heading ``# Introduction``, explain the situation and the question in two or three sentences, and the two requirements for a sustainable harvest (equilibrium and ecological stability). Under a heading ``# The model``, write out the two equations above using ``$$ ... $$``.

## The data ##

Download [recovering_fishery_counts.csv](recovering_fishery_counts.csv) into your project folder. Add a heading ``# The data`` to your report, then read the data in.

```{r}
# Read in the survey data. N is in thousands of fish
counts <- read.csv("recovering_fishery_counts.csv")

# Have a look at the first six years
head(counts)

```

There's one row for each year, and one column for each of the four survey zones, holding the estimated number of fish in thousands. We want the size of the whole stock, so let's add the four zones together into a new column.

```{r}
# Total number of fish (thousands) across all four zones in each year
counts$total <- counts$zone_A + counts$zone_B + counts$zone_C + counts$zone_D

# The number of years of surveys
n_years <- nrow(counts)

```

Now we can use subsetting to pull out the first and last surveys. Remember that inside the square brackets, whatever goes before the comma picks the rows and whatever goes after it picks the columns. Instead of saying *which* row number we want, we can describe *what* the rows we want look like.

```{r}
# The total in the first survey (1985) and the most recent survey (2025)
N_1985 <- counts[counts$year == 1985, "total"]
N_2025 <- counts[counts$year == 2025, "total"]

# How many times bigger is the stock now?
N_2025 / N_1985

```

Read that first line out loud as "give me the ``total`` column, from the rows of ``counts`` where ``year`` is equal to 1985". Note that it's two equals signs, ``==``, which asks "is this equal to?". A single ``=`` is for giving values to arguments.

A table of every tenth year makes a nice summary for a report. ``%in%`` asks "is this value one of these?", so it keeps the rows whose year is in our list. ``knitr::kable()`` then turns the result into a proper table when you knit.

```{r}
# Keep the rows from every tenth year, and turn them into a table for the report
knitr::kable(counts[counts$year %in% c(1985, 1995, 2005, 2015, 2025), ], row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Survey estimates (thousands of fish) every ten years.")

```

Now let's plot the recovery. In Week 2 we had to save each plot to a file with ``dev.copy()``. In R Markdown there's no need, plots go straight into the report. To give a plot a caption, add ``fig.cap`` to the chunk options, like the example in the chunk options section above.

```{r recovery-plot, fig.cap="Total survey estimates for the fishery since fishing was banned in 1985."}
# Plot the total stock over time
plot(counts$year, counts$total,
     pch = 19,
     xlab = "Year",
     ylab = "Number of fish (thousands)",
     main = "Recovery of the fishery after the 1985 ban")

```

**In your report:** describe the recovery in a sentence or two, using inline code for the numbers. For example, mine says "Between 1985 and 2025 the stock grew from `r N_1985` to `r N_2025` thousand fish." and in my ``.Rmd`` file that sentence looks like this:

````md
Between 1985 and 2025 the stock grew from `r knitr::inline_expr("N_1985")` to `r knitr::inline_expr("N_2025")` thousand fish.
````

## Estimating the carrying capacity ##

Look at the plot. The stock grows quickly at first and then levels off. That levelling off is the carrying capacity ``K``, just like the paramecium last week. To estimate ``K``, we take the mean of the surveys once the stock has levelled off. From the plot, that's from about 2000 onwards. Subsetting again!

```{r}
# Keep only the years after the stock levelled off
plateau <- counts[counts$year >= 2000, ]

# Carrying capacity K: the mean total from those years
K <- mean(plateau$total)
K

```

The surveys bounce either side of ``K`` from year to year, which is what we'd expect if the population is sitting at its carrying capacity and the ups and downs are just good years, bad years and survey error.

**In your report:** add a heading ``# Estimating the carrying capacity``, explain how you estimated ``K`` and report it with inline code. It's also worth adding ``abline(h = K, lty = 2)`` under your recovery plot to show where ``K`` sits. Remember the chunk that calculates ``K`` has to come before the plot for this to work!

## Estimating R0 ##

Now for the trickier parameter. ``R_0`` is the per capita growth rate when the population is small and there's no crowding. The logistic model says that the per capita growth rate ``R`` falls in a straight line as the population grows:

$$R = R_0\left(1 - \frac{N}{K}\right)$$

So if we plot the observed ``R`` against ``N``, the points should fall roughly on a straight line, and where that line hits ``N = 0`` is ``R_0``. This is exactly why the early recovery years are so valuable. They are the only years when the population was small.

Just like last week, we can build a table of observed growth from one year to the next. Notice the negative numbers inside the square brackets. A minus sign means "everything **except** this one", so ``[-n_years]`` drops the last year and ``[-1]`` drops the first.

```{r}
# Population size this year, N(t). We drop the last year because there is no
# following year to compare it to
N_t <- counts$total[-n_years]

# Population size next year, N(t+1). We drop the first year so everything lines up
N_t1 <- counts$total[-1]

# A table of the observed growth from each year to the next
growth <- data.frame(
  year = counts$year[-n_years],
  N = N_t,
  # Observed natural growth G(N). No fishing, so this is just the change in N
  G_obs = N_t1 - N_t,
  # Observed per capita growth rate R = G(N) / N
  R_obs = (N_t1 - N_t) / N_t
)

# The first ten years of the recovery, when the population was small
growth[growth$year < 1995, ]

```

Now we fit a straight line through ``R_obs`` against ``N``. In Excel you would have added a linear trendline to your chart. In R, the line of best fit comes from the function ``lm()``, which stands for linear model. The ``~`` reads as "explained by", so ``R_obs ~ N`` means "R_obs explained by N".

```{r R-plot, fig.cap="Observed per capita growth rate against population size, with the line of best fit."}
# Fit a straight line through R_obs against N
fit <- lm(R_obs ~ N, data = growth)

# The intercept (where the line hits N = 0) and the slope of the line
coef(fit)

# R0 is the intercept. unname() just drops the label that coef() attaches
R0 <- unname(coef(fit)[1])

# Plot the observed R against N, with the line of best fit and a line at R = 0
plot(growth$N, growth$R_obs,
     pch = 19,
     xlab = "Population size N (thousands of fish)",
     ylab = "Per capita growth rate R",
     main = "Per capita growth rate vs population size")
abline(fit, col = "blue", lwd = 2)
abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "grey40")

```

There's our straight line, falling as the population grows. The points are noisy (real data always are!), but the trend is clear. Here's a neat check. The line crosses ``R = 0`` at ``N = -intercept / slope``, which is the logistic model's carrying capacity. Our line crosses at `r round(-coef(fit)[1] / coef(fit)[2])`, very close to the ``K`` of `r round(K)` we got from the plateau. Two different ways of estimating ``K`` agree, which gives us confidence in the model.

**In your report:** add a heading ``# Estimating R0``, explain how you estimated ``R_0`` and report it with inline code. Hint, ``round(R0, 2)`` inside your inline code will stop R giving you 15 decimal places.

## The production function ##

We now have both parameters, so we can calculate the production function ``G(N)`` for every population size from 0 to ``K``, and plot it. We'll also add our observed growth, ``G_obs``, as points, so we can see how well the model matches the data.

```{r production-plot, fig.cap="The logistic production function (line) with the observed growth from each year to the next (points)."}
# A dataframe of population sizes from 0 to K in steps of 1
production <- data.frame(N = seq(0, K, by = 1))

# Natural growth G(N) at every one of those population sizes
production$G_N <- R0 * (1 - production$N / K) * production$N

# Plot the production function as a line
plot(production$N, production$G_N,
     type = "l",
     lwd = 2,
     col = "blue",
     # Make the y axis tall enough to fit all of the observed points
     ylim = range(c(production$G_N, growth$G_obs)),
     xlab = "Population size N (thousands of fish)",
     ylab = "Natural growth G(N) (thousands of fish per year)",
     main = "Production function")

# Add the observed growth as points, and a dashed line at zero
points(growth$N, growth$G_obs, pch = 19)
abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "grey40")

```

There's the hump from the lectures, and the observed growth follows it nicely. The peak of the hump is the maximum sustainable yield (MSY), the largest harvest the population could possibly sustain. We can find it with subsetting, by asking for the row where ``G(N)`` equals its largest value.

```{r}
# The row of the production function where G(N) is at its maximum
production[production$G_N == max(production$G_N), ]

# Store the MSY and the population size where it happens
MSY <- max(production$G_N)
N_MSY <- production[production$G_N == MSY, "N"]

# Check against the formulas from the lectures, MSY = R0 * K / 4 and N_MSY = K / 2
R0 * K / 4
K / 2

```

Subsetting and the formulas agree. They're not *exactly* the same, because our ``N`` values only go up in steps of 1.

**In your report:** add a heading ``# The production function``, include the plot, and report the MSY and ``N_MSY`` using inline code.

## Choosing a sustainable harvest ##

Now for the question we came here to answer. We'll compare four possible harvests: half the MSY, three quarters of the MSY, the MSY itself, and a quarter more than the MSY.

```{r}
# Four harvests to compare, in thousands of fish per year
harvests <- c(0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.25) * MSY
round(harvests)

```

### Finding the equilibria ###

From the lectures, a harvest ``h`` has an equilibrium wherever ``G(N) = h``. On the production function, that's wherever a horizontal line at ``h`` crosses the hump. We can find these with subsetting. We keep every population size where natural growth can keep up with the harvest, ``G(N) >= h``, and the two ends of that range are the two equilibria.

We'll do this for all four harvests at once with a ``for loop``, storing the answers in a dataframe. There's one catch. If a harvest is bigger than the MSY, there are no population sizes that can keep up with it, so the subset has no rows. We use an ``if`` statement, just like the R version check in Week 2, to only fill in the equilibria when there are some.

```{r}
# A dataframe to hold the equilibria for each harvest. NA means "not available"
equilibria <- data.frame(h = harvests, lower = NA, upper = NA)

for (i in 1:nrow(equilibria)) {
  # Keep the population sizes where G(N) can keep up with this harvest
  can_sustain <- production[production$G_N >= equilibria$h[i], ]

  # If there are any, the smallest and largest are the two equilibria
  if (nrow(can_sustain) > 0) {
    equilibria$lower[i] <- min(can_sustain$N)
    equilibria$upper[i] <- max(can_sustain$N)
  }
}

# Turn it into a table for the report, rounded to whole numbers
knitr::kable(round(equilibria), caption = "Equilibria for each harvest (thousands of fish).")

```

Half the MSY has two equilibria that are far apart. As the harvest grows, they squeeze together, until at the MSY they meet at ``N_MSY``. Above the MSY there are none at all, which means no equilibrium and a collapse.

### Testing stability ###

Finding an equilibrium is only half the job. We also need to know whether it is ecologically stable. Just like you did in Excel, we test this by starting the population at different sizes, harvesting it every year, and watching what happens. We'll try every combination of our four harvests and six starting populations, including today's stock, over 50 years. ``expand.grid()`` makes a table of every combination.

```{r}
# Number of years to simulate
n_sim <- 50

# Every combination of six starting populations and our four harvests
scenarios <- expand.grid(N0 = c(200, 400, 600, 800, 1000, N_2025),
                         h = harvests)

```

Now we loop over the rows of ``scenarios``. For each one, we step the model forward one year at a time, just like last week, but this time subtracting the harvest. A population can't have fewer than zero fish, so ``max(0, ...)`` takes whichever is bigger, zero or the new population size. This is a loop inside a loop. The outer loop picks a scenario, and the inner loop runs it. Each run is stacked onto the bottom of a big dataframe called ``simulations`` with ``rbind()``.

```{r}
# An empty dataframe to collect every simulation
simulations <- data.frame()

for (s in 1:nrow(scenarios)) {
  # Subset out the starting population and harvest for this scenario
  N0 <- scenarios[s, "N0"]
  h <- scenarios[s, "h"]

  # Step the model forward one year at a time
  N <- numeric(n_sim + 1)
  N[1] <- N0
  for (t in 1:n_sim) {
    N[t + 1] <- max(0, N[t] + R0 * (1 - N[t] / K) * N[t] - h)
  }

  # Stack this simulation onto the bottom of the others
  simulations <- rbind(simulations, data.frame(year = 0:n_sim, N = N, N0 = N0, h = h))
}

```

Now let's plot the simulations for one harvest. We subset out the rows for that harvest, draw an empty set of axes with ``type = "n"`` (n for nothing), and then use a ``for loop`` to subset out each starting population in turn and draw it with ``lines()``. ``paste()`` glues bits of text together to make a title that changes with the harvest.

```{r stability-plot, fig.cap="The stock over 50 years from six starting populations, harvesting three quarters of the MSY. The dashed lines are the two equilibria."}
# Choose which harvest to plot, the second one is three quarters of the MSY
h_plot <- harvests[2]

# Subset out the simulations and equilibria for that harvest
sims_h <- simulations[simulations$h == h_plot, ]
eq_h <- equilibria[equilibria$h == h_plot, ]

# Draw the axes only
plot(sims_h$year, sims_h$N,
     type = "n",
     ylim = c(0, K),
     xlab = "Years after fishing reopens",
     ylab = "Number of fish (thousands)",
     main = paste("Harvest of", round(h_plot), "thousand fish per year"))

# One line for each starting population
for (start in unique(sims_h$N0)) {
  one_run <- sims_h[sims_h$N0 == start, ]
  lines(one_run$year, one_run$N, lwd = 2, col = "blue")
}

# Add the equilibria as dashed grey lines
abline(h = c(eq_h$lower, eq_h$upper), lty = 2, col = "grey40")

```

Now for the moment of truth. Every population that started **above** the lower equilibrium ended up at the upper equilibrium, so the upper equilibrium is **stable**. The population that started **below** the lower equilibrium crashed to zero, so the lower equilibrium is **unstable**. That lower equilibrium is a danger line. If the stock ever falls below it, the fishery will collapse unless the harvest is cut.

Finally, a table of how every scenario ended up. We subset out the final year, and add a column saying whether the population collapsed.

```{r}
# Keep only the final year of every simulation
final <- simulations[simulations$year == n_sim, ]

# TRUE if the population collapsed to zero
final$collapsed <- final$N == 0

# How many of the scenarios collapsed? sum() counts the TRUEs
sum(final$collapsed)

# A table of the final population for every scenario
knitr::kable(round(final[, c("h", "N0", "N")]), row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Stock after 50 years for each harvest and starting population (thousands of fish).")

```

### Your turn ###

a. Copy the plotting chunk three times and change ``h_plot`` to ``harvests[1]``, ``harvests[3]`` and ``harvests[4]``, so that your report has a plot for all four harvests. What happens at the MSY? What happens above it?
b. Which starting populations collapsed when harvesting three quarters of the MSY? Hint, subset ``final`` using ``&``.
c. **If you have time.** Our estimates of ``K`` and ``R_0`` came from noisy data, so they might be a bit off. Try knitting with ``R0`` 20% lower than your estimate (multiply it by 0.8 in the chunk where you make it). Which harvests are still sustainable? Change it back when you're done.

## Your recommendation ##

So, how much should the fishery be allowed to harvest? From the lectures and from your own simulations, a harvest is only sustainable if it is **below** the MSY and the stock stays to the **right** of the lower equilibrium. Harvesting right at the MSY isn't safe, because one bad year that knocks the stock below ``N_MSY`` is enough to start a collapse. And remember, our ``K`` and ``R_0`` are only estimates.

**In your report:** under a heading ``# Recommendation``, recommend an annual harvest for the fishery, in thousands of fish per year, and justify it using your equilibria and your simulations. There is no single right answer here, what matters is your reasoning.

```

### When knitting goes wrong ###

| Error message | What it usually means |
|---|---|
| ``object 'x' not found`` | You made ``x`` in the console but not in a chunk, or the chunk that makes it comes later in the document |
| ``could not find function "x"`` | A typo in the function name, or a package that you loaded in the console but not with ``library()`` in a chunk |
| ``cannot open file 'recovering_fishery_counts.csv'`` | The data file isn't in the same folder as your ``.Rmd`` |
| ``Duplicate chunk label`` | Two chunks have the same name. Rename one, or remove the name |
| ``unexpected symbol`` / ``unexpected ')'`` | A typo in your code, usually a missing comma, bracket or quotation mark. The error message tells you which chunk it was in |
| The ``.docx`` won't update | You still have the old ``.docx`` open in Word. Close it and knit again |
